short_definition: Intrinsic motivation is doing something because it is inherently interesting or satisfying, while extrinsic motivation is doing it to earn an outside reward or avoid a penalty, such as money, grades or praise.
explanation: Intrinsic motivation comes from the activity itself, and extrinsic motivation comes from what the activity gets you. Self-determination theory, developed by psychologists Edward Deci and Richard Ryan, proposes that intrinsic motivation grows when three needs are met: autonomy (having a choice), competence (feeling capable) and relatedness (feeling connected to others). Extrinsic motivation ranges from purely external, such as working for a bonus, to partly internalized, such as exercising because you value your health even though you don't enjoy it.

Intrinsic motivation tends to sustain effort over long periods and supports deeper learning. Extrinsic rewards are useful for getting started on tasks that aren't enjoyable. Most lasting habits combine both.

There is a trade-off in each direction. Research on the 'overjustification effect' suggests that adding external rewards to an activity people already enjoy can sometimes reduce their interest in it. On the other hand, waiting until you feel motivated before acting can stall progress. Sometimes external structure, such as a deadline or a commitment to someone else, is exactly what gets you going.
example: Illustrative example: Two people start learning to code. Alex is motivated only by a promised raise, and when the raise is delayed, Alex stops practicing. Jordan also wants the raise but picks projects that are fun, such as automating a hobby spreadsheet, and tracks small wins along the way. When the raise is delayed, Jordan keeps practicing because the work itself has become rewarding.
common_mistake: Relying only on rewards such as treats or purchases to stay motivated, then losing momentum when the reward stops or starts to feel routine.
title: Intrinsic vs Extrinsic Motivation
